q: Australia has the world's largest herd of which animal living wild, first imported in the 1800s?
fact: Camels were shipped in to carry goods across the outback. Hundreds of thousands now roam free, and some are even exported to the Middle East.

q: Which egg-laying mammal with a duck-like bill lives only in Australia?
fact: Males carry a venomous spur on each hind leg. When the first specimen reached Europe, scientists suspected it was a hoax.

q: What is the Aboriginal name of the giant red rock in central Australia once known as Ayers Rock?
fact: Uluru rises 348 meters above the desert plain and is sacred to the Anangu people. Climbing it has been banned since 2019.

q: Which dark, salty spread made from brewer's yeast is an Australian breakfast icon?
fact: Vegemite was invented in Melbourne in 1922 as a way to use up the yeast left over from brewing.

q: Australia's capital Canberra was built from scratch as a compromise between which two rival cities?
fact: Neither city would accept the other as capital, so a brand-new one was founded in 1913 on farmland between them.

q: Which Australian sporting event is known as 'the race that stops a nation'?
fact: The horse race is run on the first Tuesday of November, and the day is a public holiday in Melbourne.

q: What did Australia build, stretching more than 5,000 km, to keep dingoes away from its sheep?
fact: The Dingo Fence runs about 5,600 km from Queensland to the southern coast - one of the longest structures on Earth.

q: The Australian coat of arms shows a kangaroo and which bird?
fact: Neither animal walks backward easily - a popular explanation for why they were chosen to stand for a nation moving forward.

q: What is the Māori name for New Zealand, often translated as 'land of the long white cloud'?
fact: The Māori-language version of the national anthem, usually sung before the English one, is titled 'Aotearoa'.

q: Which flightless bird gives New Zealanders their nickname?
fact: For its size the kiwi lays one of the largest eggs of any bird - up to a fifth of the female's body weight.

q: Which Māori ceremonial dance does New Zealand's national rugby team perform before its matches?
fact: The best-known haka, 'Ka Mate', was composed around 1820 by the chief Te Rauparaha.

q: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give what to women?
fact: Suffragist Kate Sheppard led the campaign. Today her portrait is on New Zealand's ten-dollar note.

q: Which film trilogy, shot across New Zealand, left behind a hobbit village near the town of Matamata?
fact: The Hobbiton set was later rebuilt in permanent materials and now draws visitors from all over the world.

q: Which fuzzy fruit, originally from China, was renamed and made famous by New Zealand growers?
fact: It was known as the Chinese gooseberry until exporters renamed it after the national bird in 1959.

q: What unusual status did New Zealand grant the Whanganui River in 2017?
answer: The legal rights of a person
wrong: A ban on all boat traffic
fact: The law reflects the Māori view of the river as an ancestor. Two appointed guardians speak on its behalf.

q: What is a hāngi in traditional Māori cooking in New Zealand?
answer: Food steamed in an earth oven
wrong: Meat dried in the sea wind
fact: Baskets of meat and vegetables are buried in a pit over heated stones and left to cook for several hours.

q: At which Olympics did Fiji win its first-ever medal, a gold in rugby sevens?
fact: Fiji beat Great Britain 43-7 in the final and later honored the team on a rare seven-dollar banknote.

q: Which famous line runs straight across the Fijian island of Taveuni?
fact: The International Date Line was bent around Fiji, so the whole country keeps one date even though the meridian cuts through it.

q: What does the everyday Fijian greeting 'Bula' literally mean?
fact: The longer formal greeting, 'Ni sa bula vinaka', wishes the listener good health and happiness.

q: Kiribati's islands lie in how many of Earth's four hemispheres?
fact: Its 33 islands straddle both the Equator and the 180th meridian, scattered over an ocean area about the size of India.

q: How is the name of Kiribati correctly pronounced?
fact: In the Gilbertese language 'ti' is pronounced like 's'. The name is simply the local spelling of 'Gilberts'.

q: Kiritimati in Kiribati is one of the world's largest coral atolls. What does its name mean?
fact: Captain Cook arrived there on Christmas Eve 1777. Kiritimati is how 'Christmas' is spelled in Gilbertese.

q: Which piece of clothing was named after an atoll in the Marshall Islands in 1946?
fact: French designer Louis Réard named his new two-piece swimsuit after Bikini Atoll, which was making headlines that summer.

q: Navigators in the Marshall Islands traditionally mapped ocean swells using charts made of what?
fact: The sticks showed how waves bend around islands, which were marked by shells. Sailors memorized the chart and left it ashore.

q: The island of Yap in Micronesia is famous for which unusual traditional money?
fact: The largest rai stones are about 3.6 meters across. They rarely move - everyone simply remembers who owns which stone.

q: Which ruined stone city, built on about 100 artificial islets, lies off Pohnpei in Micronesia?
fact: Its walls are stacked from basalt columns, some weighing many tons. Nan Madol became a World Heritage Site in 2016.

q: Unusually for a country, Nauru has no official what?
fact: The government offices sit in the Yaren district, which serves as the capital in practice.

q: Nauru once grew rich by mining which substance, formed over ages from seabird droppings?
fact: In the 1970s phosphate briefly gave Nauru one of the highest incomes per person in the world.

q: About how long does it take to drive all the way around Nauru on its coastal ring road?
fact: The ring road is only about 19 km long. Nauru is the smallest island nation in the world.

q: Why can snorkelers swim safely among the golden jellyfish of Palau's Jellyfish Lake?
answer: Their sting is too weak to feel
wrong: They only come out at night
They are kept behind safety nets
They stay near the lake bottom
fact: Cut off from the sea, the jellyfish spend each day following the sun back and forth across the lake.

q: In 2009 Palau created the world's first national sanctuary for which animals?
fact: The sanctuary banned commercial shark fishing across all of Palau's waters, an area roughly the size of France.

q: What must every visitor to Palau sign, stamped into their passport on arrival?
wrong: A promise to learn a greeting
A vow to visit every island
A receipt for a visitor tax
fact: The Palau Pledge, introduced in 2017, is addressed to the children of Palau and was written with their help.

q: Papua New Guinea has more of what than any other country - over 800 of them?
fact: Steep mountains and dense forest kept communities apart, so more than a tenth of the world's languages are spoken here.

q: Which bird flies on the flag of Papua New Guinea?
fact: The flag was designed in 1971 by 15-year-old schoolgirl Susan Karike. It also shows the Southern Cross.

q: The hooded pitohui of Papua New Guinea is one of the very few birds in the world that are what?
fact: Its skin and feathers carry the same kind of toxin found in poison dart frogs, picked up from the beetles it eats.

q: Why did Samoa skip December 30, 2011 entirely, going straight from the 29th to the 31st?
answer: It moved across the date line
fact: The jump put Samoa on the same day as its main trading partners, Australia and New Zealand.

q: Which Scottish author of 'Treasure Island' spent his final years in Samoa and is buried there?
fact: Samoans called him Tusitala, 'teller of tales'. His grave lies on Mount Vaea above his former home.

q: In 2009 Samoa became the first country in decades to change which road rule?
answer: The side of the road to drive on
fact: Samoa switched from right to left so that cheaper used cars could be imported from Australia and New Zealand.

q: On which island does Honiara, the capital of Solomon Islands, stand?
fact: Guadalcanal is the country's largest island. A Spanish explorer named it after his hometown in Andalusia.

q: On Malaita in Solomon Islands, what is traditional money made from?
fact: Shell money is still made by hand in Langa Langa Lagoon and exchanged at weddings and other ceremonies.

q: What sets Tonga's history apart from every other Pacific island nation?
wrong: It never joined the United Nations
fact: Tonga became a British protected state in 1900 but kept its own king and government throughout.

q: What nickname did Captain Cook give to Tonga after the warm welcome he received there in the 1770s?
fact: The name stuck: Tonga still calls itself the Friendly Islands when it welcomes visitors today.

q: In Tonga, what is the ta'ovala that people wear around the waist on formal occasions?
fact: Wearing a ta'ovala is a sign of respect, a bit like a suit and tie. Old family mats are treasured heirlooms.

q: Tuvalu earns millions of dollars a year from which lucky internet asset?
wrong: Its rights to a satellite orbit
fact: The country code .tv happens to be perfect for video sites, and licensing it brings in a sizable share of government revenue.

q: The name Tuvalu means 'eight standing together'. What are the eight?
fact: A ninth island, tiny Niulakita, was settled only in 1949 - which is why the flag carries nine stars.

q: In Tuvalu's capital Funafuti, what do locals use as a sports field and meeting place in the evenings?
fact: With only a few flights a week and almost no spare land, the runway doubles as the island's biggest open space.

q: Which extreme sport was inspired by the land-diving ritual of Pentecost Island in Vanuatu?
fact: Each year men leap from wooden towers up to 30 meters tall with only vines tied to their ankles.

q: Off Hideaway Island in Vanuatu, snorkelers can visit which unusual public service?
fact: Opened in 2003 about three meters below the surface, it accepts special waterproof postcards.

q: Before independence in 1980, Vanuatu was jointly ruled by Britain and France under what name?
fact: The shared rule meant two police forces, two school systems and two sets of laws on the same islands.

q: Which Pacific island nation is the world's smallest republic by area?
fact: At 21 square km, Nauru is smaller than many airports. Only Vatican City and Monaco are smaller countries.

q: Which country was the last large landmass on Earth to be settled by humans, only about 700 years ago?
fact: Polynesian voyagers arrived by canoe around 1250-1300. Australia, by contrast, has been inhabited for over 50,000 years.

q: Which country takes up an entire continental mainland all by itself?
fact: That mainland is the flattest and the driest of all the inhabited continents.

q: Which country is crossed by the Kokoda Track, a 96 km jungle trail over the Owen Stanley Range?
fact: Walking the steep, muddy track takes most hikers between four and ten days.

q: Which country's flag shows a frigatebird flying over a sun rising from ocean waves?
fact: The three white waves stand for the country's three island groups: the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands.

q: Which country's two main islands are called Viti Levu and Vanua Levu?
fact: 'Viti' is the local name for the country itself. The English name comes from how neighboring Tongans pronounced it.

q: Which country was known to early European explorers as the Navigator Islands?
fact: French explorer Bougainville chose the name in 1768 after seeing islanders handle their canoes far out at sea.

q: Which country is known for its Rock Islands, hundreds of mushroom-shaped limestone islets in a turquoise lagoon?
fact: Waves and sea creatures have eaten away the base of each islet, leaving them looking like green mushrooms.

q: Which country consists of two parallel island chains named Ratak and Ralik, meaning 'sunrise' and 'sunset'?
fact: Together the two chains hold 29 atolls and 5 single islands, with a total land area smaller than many cities.

q: Which country's national rugby team is known as the All Blacks?
fact: The name comes from the team's all-black kit, worn with a silver fern on the chest.

q: Which country is home to Mount Yasur, a volcano on Tanna island that has erupted almost nonstop for centuries?
fact: Its glow is said to have drawn Captain Cook to the island in 1774. Visitors can walk right up to the crater rim.

q: Which country is the last remaining indigenous monarchy in the Pacific, ruled by its own royal family?
fact: The royal line goes back to King George Tupou I, who united the islands in 1845.

q: Which tiny animals built the Great Barrier Reef, the largest living structure on Earth?
fact: The reef stretches about 2,300 km along Australia's northeast coast and can be seen from space.

q: The Pacific islands are traditionally grouped into Polynesia, Melanesia and which third region?
fact: The names are Greek: the third one means 'small islands', while Melanesia means 'black islands'.

q: What does the name Polynesia mean?
fact: The term was coined in 1756 by French writer Charles de Brosses from the Greek 'poly' (many) and 'nesos' (island).

q: Which traditional Pacific drink is made from the ground root of a pepper plant?
fact: Kava is shared from a common bowl at ceremonies in Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and Vanuatu, and leaves the lips slightly numb.

q: The English word 'tattoo' comes from 'tatau', a word from which family of languages?
fact: Captain Cook's crew brought the word home from Tahiti in 1769. In Samoa the art of tatau is still practiced by hand.

q: Which trench in the western Pacific contains the deepest known point in any ocean?
fact: The Challenger Deep lies nearly 11 km down - deep enough to swallow Mount Everest with 2 km to spare.

q: In what kind of boat did Polynesian navigators cross thousands of kilometers of open ocean?
fact: Without instruments, they steered by the stars, the swells, the clouds and the flight paths of birds.

q: The Polynesian Triangle has Hawaii and New Zealand at two corners. What lies at the third?
fact: Tahiti and Samoa lie inside the triangle, whose sides are each around 7,000 km long.

q: The meringue dessert pavlova, claimed by both Australia and New Zealand, is named after a famous what?
fact: Anna Pavlova toured both countries in the 1920s, and they have argued over who invented her dessert ever since.
